articles.title: Claude comes for Gemini with its own take on Docs and Slides
articles.summary: Anthropic’s “one Claude” update combines regular Claude chats and Cowork, alongside the launch of new Claude Docs and Slides tools.
articles.body: Claude is getting a pair of new tools today: Docs and Slides. They’ll let you create documents and presentations through Claude chats, which you can export, edit, and share with other users. As part of the announcement, Anthropic is also simplifying how Claude chats work, merging regular chats and Cowork into “one Claude,” with all of its AI productivity tools available from any chat. Artifacts and Claude Design capabilities will be available through the new single interface as well. According to Anthropic, Claude “can now figure out what a task needs, so what Cowork and Design can do is available from any conversation, with the context, skills, and connectors you already have.” Claude Docs and Slides are launching in beta, joining Claude Design as part of the AI platform’s productivity tools. You can have Claude generate documents and presentations from any chat. You can ask Claude to make changes to whatever it creates, or make edits manually. [Image: Like Google Docs, Claude Docs start as private documents, but you can share them with other editors who can work on the document at the same time as you. Collaborators, including Claude, can leave comments that look like those on a Google Doc. Anthropic says “Anything you make with Claude Design, Slides, or Docs lives at one shareable link you can open on your phone.” Anthropic’s models are generally seen as more advanced than Google’s, but Google’s AI services have the advantage of being natively tied into its suite of productivity tools. Earlier this year, Google expanded Gemini’s role in Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides with features like a Gemini chat window in Docs, generating and editing entire documents with Gemini, and creating slides with Gemini. The addition of Docs and Slides to Claude starts to close the gap between Anthropic’s AI platform and Google’s productivity tools, giving users fewer reasons to leave a Claude chat for other tools. The “one Claude” update is rolling out first to Pro and Max users on web, desktop, and mobile “over the next few weeks,” with access for Team and Free users coming later. Anthropic says there’s “nothing to turn on” for the update, and users can also keep using Claude chat normally.

articles.title: Anthropic merges Claude chat and Cowork in one interface
articles.summary: Anthropic is initially releasing these features to Pro and Max plan subscribers.
articles.body:
Anthropic is merging its front end for Claude chat and Cowork, making it less confusing for people to decide which tab to use for different tasks.

The unified interface lets users access chat, Cowork, and Artifacts (Claude’s interactive workspace feature) within one window. Claude Design, which was introduced in April for website and prototype design, also works anywhere within Claude.

Before this rollout, the company said customers often struggled to choose the right tab for the right task. With the new design, Claude automatically routes requests without having to switch tabs or windows. The idea is to remove confusion about which feature to pick and use just one front end to route work to different parts of the app.

Hopefully, OpenAI also takes a cue from this rollout and fixes ChatGPT’s interface across the platforms.

Anthropic is also adding dedicated features for making presentations and documents. Users can ask the AI assistant to create, edit, and present slides, and it can also download the generated presentation as a PDF or PowerPoint.

Similarly, with the Docs feature, users can work alongside Claude to create sections, ask questions, and comment on completed parts. Users can share generated documents or slides with a link and edit them on their phone.

Users can also ask Claude to start creating a document on desktop, and they can check the progress of the task using the mobile app.

These features are rolling out to Claude’s Pro and Max plans first, on the web, desktop, and mobile over the coming weeks. The company plans to extend them to the free and team tiers later.

The update comes in the wake of an upgrade of Cowork’s memory layer , which helps Claude remember user context across chats.

articles.title: Joe Rogan hopes artificial intelligence will take over government, military decisions
articles.summary: Joe Rogan said on "The Joe Rogan Experience" that AI should govern foreign policy and end wars, but Amy Kremer says machines lack accountability.
articles.body: Joe Rogan said Tuesday that he hopes artificial intelligence could eventually take over government and foreign-policy functions, including decisions involving military conflict, as he believes AI could help prevent wars that human leaders have failed to stop. Rogan, speaking with theoretical physicist Carlo Rovelli during a conversation on "The Joe Rogan Experience," acknowledged that handing government functions to artificial intelligence could alarm people but described it as a possible way to remove human decision-making from international conflicts. "It sounds like a crazy hope, but my hope is that as AI becomes more and more omnipresent, as we start farming off various tasks to it, one of the things that we're going to farm off is government," Rogan said. "One of the things we're going to farm off is how we interact with other countries. I know that's terrifying to people, but just think of the disastrous effects that we've had so far with humans doing it." UNITED ARAB EMIRATES PLANS AI-RUN GOVERNMENT WITHIN TWO YEARS Republican National Committee National Committeewoman for Georgia and Humans First Chairwoman Amy Kremer, who has pushed for greater safeguards around AI while opposing a blanket halt to American development of the technology, rejected Rogan's proposal. "Hell no. Joe Rogan is way off base," Kremer said in a Wednesday statement to Fox News Digital. "AI is a tool, not a governing authority. These are machines. They have no soul, no conscience, no moral judgment and no accountability to the American people." "AI can certainly assist human beings by analyzing information and helping policymakers make better-informed decisions. But there is a profound difference between using AI as a tool and surrendering human decision-making to it," she continued. MIKE JOHNSON REJECTS AI MORATORIUM OVER CHINA THREAT AS CONSERVATIVE ACTIVIST DEMANDS GUARDRAILS Rogan specifically imagined AI intervening in military conflict, suggesting the technology could one day halt wars around the world. "If all international military conflicts ended instantaneously upon AI governing the use of conflicts and military weapons... imagine that. Imagine a war where it stops. All war stops on the planet. That is one of the things that everybody wants, but no one thinks could ever possibly happen," Rogan said. Kremer said decisions involving military force and individual rights should remain subject to human accountability. "Decisions about war and peace, foreign policy, our constitutional rights and the exercise of government power must always remain in human hands," she said. "If a decision can take a life, take away someone’s liberty, or fundamentally affect the American people, a human being must make that decision and be accountable for it." ANTHROPIC CEO LIKENS AI FIGHT WITH CHINA TO COLD WAR, SEEKS 'DISARMAMENT NEGOTIATIONS' The exchange came amid a rapidly escalating national debate over how much authority should be delegated to increasingly capable AI systems. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for slowing development of frontier AI on Saturday, drawing support from Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Altman separately warned that humanity losing control of the future of AI would be "unacceptable." The Trump administration has moved to accelerate the military and intelligence community's adoption of AI while keeping responsibility within the existing chain of command. A June White House national security memorandum requires national-security AI systems to be controllable and directs that commanders, agency directors and other officials remain accountable for their use. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Kremer said the line between technological assistance and governing authority should remain clear. "Technology should serve humanity. Humanity should never serve the machines," Kremer said.

articles.title: Google will now let any AI agent run your smart home
articles.summary: Google’s new Model Context Protocol integration lets AI agents like Claude and OpenClaw control your Google Home devices and data.
articles.body: Google is opening up its smart home to AI agents, letting tools like Claude and Open Claw access and control your connected devices and analyze your home’s data using the standardized Model Context Protocol. Google Home MCP is a new integration that lets third-party AI agents control and monitor your smart home and act on your behalf. It “allows any AI agents that support MCP, including Google Antigravity, Claude, Hermes or Open Claw, to securely work with all of the devices and event history in your Google Home ecosystem,” Taylor Lehman, group product manager at Google Home & Nest, said in a blog post. According to Lehman, Home MCP integration will connect your AI agent of choice to real-world events, enabling a host of new capabilities. From things like cross-camera analysis — so you could ask your agent what your kid did when they got home from school — to using device state history to figure out how many loads of laundry you did last week or how long the lights were left on. It will also allow your agent to interact with you via voice, for example, by sending an audio message over your Google Home speaker when it has finished a task. You can also have your agent create a custom dashboard to control your Google Home. [Image: Google Home smart speakers will still be controlled by Gemini for Home, but with MCP enabled third-party AI agents will be able to send voice messages to you through them. This doesn’t replace Google’s new Gemini for Home assistant, which remains Google’s interface for interacting with Google Home through the Home app and Google Nest smart speakers, following the demise of Google Assistant. Instead, MCP integration adds another layer of control, allowing third-party AI agents to interact directly with devices connected to Google Home through their own interfaces. At launch, availability is limited to Google Home Premium Advanced users in the US ($20/month or $200/year), with access rolling out in the coming weeks. Setup requires creating a Google Cloud project and configuring it to use the Home MCP. Giving an AI agent access to real-world devices like smart locks, thermostats, and core infrastructure like HVAC systems and appliances raises obvious questions about security, privacy, and safety. Google says Home MCP enforces rate limits and safety protections; for example, it won’t allow an agent to unlock doors. However, depending on your agent, “connecting it to Home MCP can result in unexpected or even undesired behavior,” said Lehman, who recommends reviewing Google’s developer policies and terms of service. Home Assistant, an open-source smart home platform, has implemented a similar MCP integration that shows what you can do when you give an agent access to your smart home system. I tested this last year to use Claude to vibe-code my smart home, and it easily handled some of the more complex tasks that most interfaces — and users, for that matter — struggle with, including troubleshooting, creating automations, designing a dashboard, and setting up more advanced configurations, all using natural language. The biggest change here isn’t that Google Home can now turn your lights on and off through your Claude app; it’s that Claude — or your agent of choice — has access to the underlying data and control layer of your home. It’s a step toward building a whole home computer for your smart home that can understand what’s happening in it, reason across its history, and take action on your behalf. And if this last week wasn’t dominated by headlines about how AI will kill us all, I’d be really excited. Still, there are real advantages to giving an AI agent access to your smart home. It can reason across the data your home generates and act on it in ways traditional smart home systems generally can’t, moving the smart home from command and control toward something more contextual and proactive, closer to actual intelligence. A system that can troubleshoot a device, suggest improvements to automations, and track and identify patterns across your home is much more useful than one that just says “I’m sorry, I can’t do that.” With Home MCP integration, Google is bringing these capabilities into Google Home. [Image: Claude created this dashboard for me in Home Assistant using MCP. With Google Home MCP enabled, it should be able to do something similar for my Google Home. While consumer-facing tools like Claude will be useful for smart home tinkerers, the bigger picture here is Google’s developer play. Over the last couple of years, Google has increasingly positioned itself as the smart home’s infrastructure layer. It launched API access to its smart home in 2024 and more recently made Gemini for Home a full-stack AI offering. All of this points toward a more B2B2C strategy: Google can provide the AI and smart home infrastructure while other companies build consumer-facing services and products on top. With this week’s announcement, Google has also opened a path for developers to use its agentic Antigravity coding tool to build custom AI agents for the smart home that tap into Google Home device data and control layer. But even if developers use a different agent, as long as they’re using Google Home, it’s a win for Google. This way, Google becomes the smart home infrastructure layer, in much the same way AWS became infrastructure for internet and software businesses. Whether smart home developers will buy into Google’s promises here is a big question. Based on the number of smart home platforms the company has launched and let die over the years — Android @ Home, Weave, Project Brillo, Works with Nest, Google Assistant — developers will have to decide whether Google has finally settled on a smart home platform it intends to stick with.

articles.title: Apple might make servers again to cash in on the AI rush
articles.summary: Apple might borrow tech from Nvidia to make a return to the server market after the Mac Mini and Mac Studio prove popular with AI developers.
articles.body: According to The Information, Apple is planning to get back into the server game and might just pair up with Nvidia to make it happen. Apple retired its Xserve line in 2011 and has largely left enterprise machines to other manufacturers since. But the growing demand for compute power as the AI industry continues to expand has apparently led the company to believe there is an opening for its powerful but efficient ARM-based M processors. Its Mac Mini and Mac Studio have proven popular with AI developers, which has led to shortages. The server product, whether it’s called Xserve or something else, likely won’t debut until 2029. Word is that it will run on two or four (depending on the model) M8 Ultra chips. Apple only just announced the M6 in August, so the M8 line is a ways out. It’s also rumored that Apple’s servers could incorporate Nvidia’s NVLink Fusion tech, which connects multiple chips together so they can operate as one. While the two companies have historically had a frosty relationship behind the scenes, recently Apple turned to Nvidia chips to power its revamped Siri servers. Incorporating NVLink could lead to further collaboration between the two, but plans could still change.

articles.title: DAVID MARCUS: Big Tech invented AI doomsday to duck real life problems
articles.summary: Big Tech's AI doomsday warnings distract from real dangers like social media addiction, Section 230 reform, and algorithmic bias, critics say.
articles.body: As if Americans didn’t have enough to worry about — making ends meet and planning for the future — the heads of the world’s largest artificial-intelligence companies are now warning that their groundbreaking technology could leave us with no future at all: We may all be dead. It really is a shame, given that we just survived climate change and COVID-19. Now this? Maybe we can just shut down AI for two weeks to flatten the curve. This week, Democrats have been jumping all over themselves to hop on board this moribund bandwagon to do what they always do — regulate industry to death and hamper growth. SANDERS PUSHES 'DEATH PENALTY' FOR CRUCIAL US INDUSTRY THAT COULD GIVE ADVANTAGE TO FOREIGN ADVERSARIES According to Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., "Congress, under both Democratic and Republican control, has been asleep at the wheel, and we now have a president whose ignorance regarding this issue is truly embarrassing." Meanwhile, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., warned that "AI technology can be very dangerous when pursued without any guardrails." But given her repeated predictions that the world will end within five years because of climate change, it’s unclear why it matters. RESEARCHER WHO DEPARTED AI ROLE OVER FEARS OF RACING INTO EXTINCTION SAYS PEOPLE ARE 'BEGGING' FOR REGULATION Look, AI is not going to destroy humanity in the next decade, as Jacob Coxon, a former employee and so-called whistleblower at Anthropic — a leading AI company — warned recently. Frankly, the notion is absurd, which is why nobody can actually explain it. One must seriously ask oneself, how exactly is AI going to kill me? Is it going to come to my house with a gun, is it going to hack the nuke codes or unleash a deadly virus? Surely, it's not that hard to have human beings as fail-safes in those scenarios. THE SURVEILLANCE CAMERA ON YOUR STREET CORNER: LAWFUL SPYING OR CONSTITUTIONALLY PROBLEMATIC? No, the dangers attendant to AI are not sci-fi fantasies of super intelligence going rogue and plotting the demise of the meat puppets. As exciting as all of that is, the real dangers are much more mundane, and much more implacable. Across the country, local school boards are struggling with whether and how to use AI in kids’ education. County commissioners are balancing the crime fighting capability of AI-driven cameras against personal freedom. And in Congress, lawmakers are debating outdated laws governing Big Tech’s liability, including Section 230 of the Communications Act, which was written in the technological stone age of 1996. FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS SEE AI REGULATION AS URGENT, RANK SAFEGUARDS AHEAD OF INNOVATION These practical applications of AI are what Americans are most concerned about, not fabulist movie scenarios meant to scare us all into handing power over the smart set, again. All the usual suspects, like Bill Gates and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, are out there saying that the threat of AI requires some kind of woke world governing body, but Americans will not accept such trampling of their freedom. Not this time. TRUMP UNLOADS ON TECH TITANS PUSHING FOR SLOWDOWN ON EMERGING INDUSTRY: ‘WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!’ At the end of the day, AI is a product. It's not magic. It's not some unstoppable force of nature. And like any product, from toothpicks to tractors, the government has a role to play in making sure it is safe for the public. Viewed from this product angle, it is easy to see why Big Tech would rather talk about esoteric threats of Armageddon than what they are doing to fight bias in their algorithms, or take the safety of children online seriously. In fact, what Big Tech is really doing is inventing a problem that isn’t there to avoid addressing the very real ones that are. Even if we did force AI companies to shut down for two months and put their servers six feet apart with masks on, it would have no impact on the actual issues that people care about regarding so-called artificial intelligence. Big Tech doomerism is a distraction, because, after all, who has time to worry about teenagers getting addicted to social media or chatbots happily cheering on suicide when the world might end in ten days? CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP What the American people need and deserve are not grand, fruitless, hand-waiving gestures that seek to halt research that probably can’t be halted anyway — certainly not in China. They need sound policy regarding the practical applications of AI. People are rightfully suspicious, and even a bit scared of AI technology. But the answers to those fears do not exist in the cloud, so to speak, but on the ground — where the virtual rubber meets the very real road. The question is not whether AI will kill us, the question is how our society will choose to use it, and human beings remain in charge of that, regardless of predictions of doom.
